title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Due by Friday, 25 September 2026
One of the tasks on the day is a literature review, and the  does it against your own reference library. This page sets up Zotero, the free and  reference manager, the way we use it in the group. If you already use Zotero, skim to Step 5 and check the settings from there on. The citation key settings in Step 7 are the group convention and are worth checking even on a library you have used for years.
Written against Zotero 10 (10.0.3, September 2026), which came out in August, and the current  release. If you run an older Zotero, update it first. Two things differ from older guides you may find online: the Sync tab in the settings is now called Account, and Better BibTeX runs on Zotero 10 even though its release notes still name older versions.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
What you are setting up

Zotero, the desktop app. It stores your references, the PDFs attached to them, and your reading highlights.
A zotero.org account with sync, so your library is backed up and available on other devices.
The Zotero Connector, a browser extension that saves papers into your library with one click.
Better BibTeX, a Zotero plugin that gives every item a stable short ID called a citation key, for example forte2022building. Citation keys are how Quarto, LaTeX and other  tools refer to items.
Two settings inside Zotero: local access for other apps on your computer, which step 8 depends on, and , which puts a citation key on your clipboard with one keystroke.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 1: Install Zotero

Go to zotero.org/download.
Download the installer for your platform and install it like any other app.
Open Zotero once so it can create its data folder.

If Zotero is already installed, update it before you continue. On macOS use Zotero, Check for Updates. On Windows use Help, Check for Updates. The steps below were checked on Zotero 10 and need Zotero 7 or newer.
Throughout this page, “Settings” means the window you open with Zotero, Settings on macOS or Edit, Settings on Windows.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
section: Step 2: Create an account and turn on sync
text:
Step 2: Create an account and turn on sync

Create a free account at zotero.org/user/register and confirm the email it sends you.
In Zotero, open Settings, Account (older versions call this tab Sync).
Sign in with your new account.
Leave the data syncing defaults as they are. Data syncing covers your references, notes, tags and highlights. It is free and has no size limit.

File syncing is a separate switch on the same tab and covers the PDFs themselves. Every account gets 300 MB of file storage for free. Keep it on with the “Zotero” option if you want to read your PDFs on a second device; decide about paid storage later if the library outgrows the free tier.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 3: Install the browser connector

In the browser you normally use, go to zotero.org/download. The page detects your browser and offers the matching connector.
Install the extension and pin its button to the toolbar.
Keep the Zotero desktop app open while you save. The connector hands items to the desktop app.

To save an item, open the paper’s page (the journal landing page, an arXiv abstract page) and click the connector button. Zotero saves the reference and, when it has access, the PDF.
Two other ways to add items, both inside Zotero: click the magic wand button and paste a DOI, ISBN, PMID or arXiv ID, or drag a PDF file into the Zotero window and check the  it reads out of it.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
section: Step 4: Know your way around the library
text:
Step 4: Know your way around the library
If you have used a reference manager before, skim this. If Zotero is your first one, ten minutes here pay off.

The left pane lists your collections. A collection is a folder you assign items to. One item can sit in several collections at once.
The middle pane lists the items in the selected collection. An item is the reference record: title, authors, year, journal, DOI.
Attachments (the PDF), notes and tags hang off an item. Click the arrow next to an item to see them.
The right pane shows the selected item’s fields. Fix obvious metadata errors as you notice them, because everything downstream builds on these fields.
Double-click an item to open its PDF in Zotero’s reader. Highlights are stored in Zotero’s database and sync like any other data.

Save two or three real papers now so you have something to test with.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
section: Step 5: Allow other apps to talk to Zotero
text:
Step 5: Allow other apps to talk to Zotero
Step 8 connects the agent to your library through a local connection on your own computer. One checkbox enables it.

Open Settings, Advanced.
Check Allow other applications on this computer to communicate with Zotero.

The connection only works for apps running on the same computer. Nothing is exposed to the internet.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 6: Install Better BibTeX
Better BibTeX is installed from a downloaded file.

In your browser, go to the Better BibTeX releases page and download the latest .xpi file. You want the file saved to disk, not opened by the browser.

SafariFirefoxChrome and Edge


Click the .xpi link. Safari downloads it to your Downloads folder. If it opens a viewer instead, right-click the link and choose Download Linked File.


Firefox tries to install .xpi files as Firefox extensions, which is the wrong target. Right-click the link and choose Save Link As.


Click the link. If the browser warns that the file may be dangerous because it is an uncommon type, choose Keep. The file is safe.



In Zotero, go to Tools, Plugins.
Click the gear icon, choose Install Plugin From File, and select the .xpi you downloaded.
Restart Zotero when prompted.

After the restart, the Settings window has a new Better BibTeX tab.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 7: Configure the citation keys
This is the step to get exactly right.
A citation key is a short, readable ID for one item, like forte2022building. Once other tools refer to your items by these keys, a key must never change. When everyone in a group generates keys the same way, a paper shared through a group library carries the same key in every member’s library, and drafts move between people without anyone rekeying citations. The formula below is the shared convention at Global Health Engineering.
Open Settings, Better BibTeX. Under Citation keys:

Set the citation key formula to:
auth.lower + year + veryshorttitle(1, 0).lower
Read left to right: the last name of the first author, lowercased; the publication year; the first meaningful word of the title, lowercased. Tiago Forte’s 2022 book “Building a Second Brain” gets the key forte2022building.
Set Automatically fill citation key after to 2 seconds. Filling writes the generated key into the item’s own Citation Key field, where it is saved and synced.
Check that Regenerate citation key when item changes is unchecked. With it unchecked, a filled key stays as it is even when you later fix a typo in the author or title, which is what you want. If it is checked, uncheck it now.

Leave the remaining defaults. Then add a Citation Key column to your item list: right-click the column header in the middle pane and tick Citation Key.
Items that were already in your library may carry keys from the old default formula. Select them, right-click, and choose Better BibTeX, Regenerate citation key. Do this now, before anything refers to the old keys.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Step 8: Set up Quick Copy

Open Settings, Export.
Under Quick Copy, set Item Format to Better BibTeX Citation Key Quick Copy.
Check that Note Format is Markdown + Rich Text and that Include Zotero Links is ticked on the  line.

From now on, selecting an item and pressing Cmd+Shift+C on macOS or Ctrl+Shift+C on Windows copies its citation key.

title: Step 7: Set up Zotero
text:
Check
Save one more paper with the connector. Within two seconds its right pane shows a Citation Key in the shape authorYEARword. Select it, press the Quick Copy shortcut, paste into any text editor, and you get the bare key. Edit the title, wait two seconds, and confirm the key did not change. If all three worked, the setup is complete, and step 8 connects it to the agent.






NoteWhere this page comes from



Adapted from the Zotero getting-started guide written for the Global Health Engineering group in July 2026, shortened to what the workshop needs and checked against Zotero 10 in September 2026.

text:
Create the repository
Once you are a member, create a new repository in the agentsforsci-ghe organization.
The name should broadly reflect what you work with, following three rules:

lowercase letters only
at most two words
words separated by a dash

For example: solidwaste-kampala.
Two settings to choose on the same screen:

Visibility: public if you can, private if you cannot
Initialise this repository with: tick Add a README file

Visibility. Choose public if the data allows it. The aim is for every repository to be public by the end, so the work and its outcomes can be shown to others. If you are not ready to make yours public yet, start private and switch it later under Settings. What you must not do is treat private as permission to  something sensitive: the rule below applies either way.
README. Ticking Add a README file means GitHub creates the repository with a file already in it, so you can  it straight away. Without it you get an empty repository and a set of setup commands instead.

title: Step 1: Create your repository and add your data
text:
Add a folder called data
Inside your cloned repository, create a folder named data, and put the dataset you plan to work with into it.
What to bring. Something real from your own research, small enough to look at in one sitting. Several files are okay with a few hundred to a few thousand rows and columns you can explain. It does not need to be tidy or finished. Messy real data could be very useful here. Any file format is okay: CSV or XLSX, also PDF and DOCX, or JSON, etc.






ImportantThis must be non-sensitive data, with no personal data in it



Personal and sensitive data never go into a Git repository, private repositories included. Git  is permanent, and a later visibility change, a new collaborator, or a  to the wrong remote can expose it.
Do not commit names, recruitment or participant data, health data, signed consent, or anything that identifies a person in combination with other columns.
This matters more with an  than without one: a coding agent reads whole directories and sends file contents to a model, so protected data in the folder can leave your machine without you deciding to send it.
If you are unsure which category your data falls into, treat it as protected and ask before committing anything.

title: Agents for Scientists
text:
Background
In the first workshop you learned to use Git and GitHub so that every change to a project is versioned, documented, and open to review. This workshop puts a coding agent inside that same workflow.
The day runs the real work of writing a paper (analysing data, preparing a literature review, publishing a manuscript) under three conditions: as you do it now without agents, with an agent given minimal input, and with an agent given a proper plan and using GitHub issues. Comparing the three shows what the agent actually does for you, how you can document the process, and how you stay involved in making decisions.
Because the work runs through Git and GitHub, every action an agent takes and every decision you make is recorded as you go. That record is what makes agent use traceable and declarable, which is the second half of the day: research integrity bodies are writing  rules for scientific research right now. We will not write a response to them in the room, but what the day shows feeds into the reproducibility community’s contribution, through the AI working group of the Global Federation of Reproducibility Networks.
Four short background pages cover the themes the introduction block builds on: security, literacy, transparency, and disclosure. Reading them before the day is useful, not required.

title: Transparency
text:
The ETH integrity guidelines rest on reliability, honesty, respect, and responsibility. Reliability includes transparency and traceability, and authorship requires a significant contribution through personal work (ETH Zurich, 2026).
None of this was written with agents in mind, and none of it needs rewriting because of them. The question the workshop answers is a practical one: how do you keep faith with these principles when an agent writes some of the code and some of the prose?

text:
The ETH integrity guidelines rest on reliability, honesty, respect, and responsibility. Reliability includes transparency and traceability, and authorship requires a significant contribution through personal work (ETH Zurich, 2026).
None of this was written with agents in mind, and none of it needs rewriting because of them. The question the workshop answers is a practical one: how do you keep faith with these principles when an agent writes some of the code and some of the prose?

title: Transparency
text:
Attribution at the commit level
The answer this group is testing is that the record should be a by-product of the work rather than something reconstructed afterwards.
Every commit says what changed and who made the change. Agent commits carry a trailer, a line at the end of the , marking them as assisted; human commits carry one marking them as human-authored. The prompts behind agent commits can be archived alongside the code, so the instruction that produced a change sits next to the change.
The  then shows the whole  in one view: what the human drafted, what the agent altered, and what was reviewed before it was merged.
This is not hypothetical. The blog post that first set out this argument was written that way: a human first draft, agent edits in a second commit, prompts archived verbatim (Schöbitz, 2026a).
The talk at the Data Stewardship Network autumn meeting on 22 September 2026 took the record one step further (Schöbitz, 2026c). The deck was built with the agent, and at the end the agent was asked to write the  of AI use for it. It read the archived prompts, the commit trailers, and the line by line history of the deck file, and produced the declaration page, with the prompt that produced it archived in turn (Schöbitz, 2026b). Both are online. The same step, letting the agent write the declaration from the record, is demonstrated live on the day.
The same pattern appears elsewhere, notably Wickham committing after each AI-assisted edit so that every change is visible as a  (Wickham, 2026).

title: Transparency
section: Could you recreate it if the AI were gone?
text:
Could you recreate it if the AI were gone?
A useful test for any artifact an agent helped produce. It is fine that the AI made it. The problem is when the AI has to stay in the loop for you to be able to change it.
The failure cases are recognisable:

a dashboard nobody can reconfigure
a manuscript with citations baked into the text rather than managed
figures an agent copied from one folder to another, with no code that would remake them

The remedy is a code-based source of truth that reads the data and builds the output, so a human can rerun it. This is the same argument as reproducibility, arriving from a different direction.

title: Transparency
section: A watermark says a machine was involved, and nothing else
text:
A watermark says a machine was involved, and nothing else
Since August 2026 Anthropic marks Claude output, in line with the EU AI Act’s transparency obligation (Anthropic, 2026; European Union, 2024). Text carries a  woven into the wording itself; images and other files carry signed  attached as . Models launched from 2 August 2026 mark their output from the start, and older models follow during a transition period, so the output of a given session may or may not be marked yet.
The limits are worth knowing (Carpenter, 2026). A mark can be stripped or edited away, which is easier with the metadata on an image than with a watermark woven into text. It needs a substantial amount of text to work at all. Most importantly it carries no intent: it cannot distinguish translating your own ideas from having the machine write them, which is precisely the distinction that matters for integrity.
The audit trail from a version-controlled workflow carries what the mark cannot: what the tool did, on which files, in response to which instruction.






NoteThe short version



Traceability is not an extra step bolted onto agent use. Done this way it is the ordinary output of working through Git, and it is what makes the  question answerable rather than a matter of memory.

title: Literacy
text:
Every model produces some defective output. Useful use therefore requires enough expertise to tell good output from bad. The person, not the model, is what makes the output usable.
Cory Doctorow’s corollary is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly (Doctorow, 2026): a student is by definition not yet an expert in the subject, so learning a subject from a chatbot is incoherent. An expert can use the tool to generate and validate material precisely because they can accept or reject what comes back.
For this workshop, the practical reading is that the agent is most useful on work you could have done yourself but would rather not, and least trustworthy exactly where you cannot check it.

title: Literacy
text:
The question that matters
The anchor story from academic libraries: a student brought a polished outline generated by a chatbot and asked, “How do I know if this is actually right?” (Jiang, 2026)
That is the right question, and answering it is a skill separate from producing the output. AI literacy is an extension of information literacy: where did this come from, can I verify it, does it support my work.
Citation literacy is worth separating from citation mechanics here. Reference managers already showed that automating the format can hide whether anyone understood the source. Citation is about transparency and honesty; formatting was never the purpose.
On detection: AI text detectors cannot reliably identify AI-written text, and building integrity policy on them does not work (Jiang, 2026). The better design is work where people demonstrate their thinking through drafts, process, and transparency about what they used, which is what a version-controlled workflow like Git produces anyway.

title: Literacy
section: Skills erode when you outsource them
text:
Skills erode when you outsource them
Skill retention drops when the tool does the work. Vicki Boykis’s proposed remedy is deliberate friction, for example reading every  the agent produces. Her formulation: we should be more tired than the model (Boykis, 2026).
This is not an argument against using agents. It is an argument for choosing where the friction goes. Reading the diff is slower than accepting it, and that slowness is where the understanding lives.

title: Literacy
section: Write down what you know about your data
text:
Write down what you know about your data
If you use an agent for data analysis, you have to write down what you know about the data so the agent can help. Hadley Wickham’s point is that this is not new work invented for machines (Wickham, 2026): the data dictionary is the same documentation that always helped human colleagues, and mostly did not get written.
His working method keeps three things in sync: the cleaning script, a data dictionary, and the data file itself, with a  after each AI-assisted edit.
The workshop tests this directly. The same agent gets a plain CSV, then gets the same data published as a documented : the data together with its documentation, the column descriptions and the origin, in a form the agent can read alongside the file. The difference in what it can do is the argument for documentation.






NoteThe short version



The agent is a lever, not a substitute for knowing your field. It works best where you could check it and worst where you cannot. Documentation you write for a colleague turns out to be documentation the agent needs too.

title: Disclosure
text:
European Commission living guidelines (European Commission, 2026), six recommendations for researchers. Three shape this workshop: stay responsible for the output; use AI transparently and name the tools used substantially in the methods section, where basic editing support does not count as substantial; protect privacy, confidentiality, and intellectual property. The others ask you to respect the law, to keep learning the tools, and, the one that bites first for anyone who reviews, not to use generative AI substantially in sensitive activities such as peer review.
ETH: declare AI use (ETH Zurich, 2024). For theses the  of originality covers it. Undeclared use can trigger disciplinary proceedings.
ETH Library on citation (ETH Library, 2025): output from generative AI cannot be attributed to an author and is not a citable source. AI tools must be declared, and a missing declaration counts as ghostwriting.
That last point catches people out. You do not cite the model as a source; you declare the tool as a method. These are different things and the distinction is not merely formal, since a model recalls patterns rather than retrieving documents. Some tools write the claim first and attach citations afterwards, which is research done backwards, and whether the link back to a source is real depends entirely on how the tool was built.

title: Disclosure
text:
The standard under construction
The Focus Track of the World Conference on Research Integrity 2026, supported by the International Science Council, STM, COPE, and the Global Young Academy, is working toward a global reporting standard for AI  (International Science Council, 2026; Weaver, Seghers, et al., 2026). Round 2 of the consultation runs on a preparatory reading published in July (Weaver, McNeice, et al., 2026) and closes on 16 October 2026. The specifics below come from that document.
The proposed threshold is qualitative rather than numerical:

AI use should be disclosed if it substantively shapes or replaces human judgement, or has another substantive influence on research processes or its reporting.

The test for “substantive” is whether a disciplinary peer would reasonably need to know in order to understand how the work was done or judge whether it is reliable. Spellchecking, grammar, and formatting are named as generally not requiring disclosure. The document argues explicitly that a percentage threshold is unworkable, because there is no objective way to compute what proportion of an output an AI influenced (Weaver, McNeice, et al., 2026).
The proposed taxonomy is a controlled list of 18 research and reporting tasks (Weaver, McNeice, et al., 2026), from idea generation and literature search through data cleaning and analysis to drafting, translation, and editing. Project management and funding acquisition are deliberately excluded, on the grounds that AI use there does not affect what the article reports.
Open questions the consultation asks: where disclosure belongs (spread through the relevant sections, or gathered in one statement), whether a null statement should be mandatory the way conflict-of-interest statements are, and how to describe the verification and oversight that was actually done.

title: Disclosure
text:
Two positions to argue out
Disclose if AI was used at all. A threshold each author judges for themselves invites under-reporting, particularly given evidence that disclosing AI use lowers reader trust (Weaver, Seghers, et al., 2026), which is a standing incentive to say nothing. A version-controlled workflow logs every use anyway, so the marginal cost of full disclosure is near zero. Beyond the declaration, hand over the artifacts:  , prompts, review record.
A yes-or-no flag loses the intent. The transparency page makes the argument in full: a mark cannot tell translation of your own ideas from ghostwriting (Carpenter, 2026). Two consequences follow for disclosure. Readers will read the flag as a quality signal the way they read journal rank, and a binary requirement singles out AI as uniquely requiring negative disclosure, which may lock in a practice that looks strange once these tools are ordinary.
Where they meet: the binary rule decides whether there is something to show. The artifacts show what was actually done. Neither substitutes for the other.






NoteThe short version



The rules that exist say: declare it, stay responsible, do not cite the model as a source. The rules being written are still open on threshold, placement, and how to describe oversight. Watching agents work through a real task, with the full record in front of you, is a good way to form a view on all three. We will not write a consultation response together. What the day shows feeds into the reproducibility community’s contribution to the standard, through the AI working group of the Global Federation of Reproducibility Networks, of which I am a member.

Read them if you would rather arrive with the arguments already in mind, or come back to them afterwards when you are deciding what to change about how you work.

title: Security
text:
Personal and sensitive data never go into a Git repository, private repositories included. Git  is permanent. A later visibility change, a new collaborator, or a  to the wrong remote can expose something committed months earlier, and removing it properly is difficult.
Never in Git: names tied to attributes, recruitment data, health data, signed consent, anything that identifies a person. When you are unsure, treat it as protected and ask.
This rule predates agents. What agents change is how easily it is broken by accident: Claude Code reads a directory and pulls file contents into a request to a model. Protected data sitting in the project folder can leave your machine without you deciding to send it. The rule has to be in force before the first agent session, not after.

title: Security
text:
The ETH rule
ETH’s Cyber and Information Security unit sets two levels. Authorized use is the baseline and it is mandatory: use AI in line with the law and ETH directives, protect confidentiality, and never put personal or confidential data into a service that is not cleared for it. Responsible use includes authorized use and goes beyond it, meaning no personal data, no particularly sensitive personal data, and no information identifying ETH or third parties. Responsible use is highly desirable rather than mandatory.
AI systems count as external  services. At most “confidential” data may go into a cleared cloud service, and “strictly confidential” data never leaves ETH. ETH does provide data protected access to some AI services through its own cloud subscriptions, where what you enter is not used for training. Claude Code is not currently one of them, which is why the rule above applies to it in full.
Three obligations stay with you regardless of tool: you remain responsible for the output, you declare AI use, and you check every result. ETH has no standalone research guideline on this, so the nearest texts are the integrity guidelines (ETH Zurich, 2026) and the guidance written for teaching (ETH Zurich, 2024); the principles carry across.

title: Security
section: What the vendor does with your sessions
text:
What the vendor does with your sessions
On consumer plans (Free, Pro, Max), including Claude Code used from such an account, training on your conversations and coding sessions is on unless you turn it off (Anthropic, 2026). The choice is put to you at signup with the setting already switched on, so this is opt out rather than opt in. Two consequences follow for a research session:

Retention. Five years if you allow training, 30 days if you do not.
Two carve-outs that hold either way. A conversation flagged for safety review may be used regardless of your setting, and rating an output with the thumbs buttons stores that whole conversation as feedback, which may also be used regardless of your setting.

Commercial products (Claude Team, Claude Enterprise, and the API) fall under separate terms where Anthropic does not train on customer content by default, and the data processing addendum makes the customer the controller and Anthropic the processor. This split is the whole reason group access is being arranged rather than everyone signing up individually.
The European Commission’s living guidelines say the same thing from the researcher’s side: do not upload unpublished or sensitive work into an external AI system unless you have assurances it will not be used for training (European Commission, 2026).

title: Security
text:
What actually stops the agent
The agent has no special restraint built into it. It runs the same Git commands you do, which includes the destructive ones. Three things stand between it and your repository, and it is worth knowing which of them are real on the day:

The permission prompt, and the check that stands in for it. In  Claude Code asks before it runs a command or edits a file, and reading that prompt rather than approving it by reflex is the guardrail you operate yourself. On the day we work in , where a second model checks each action against a set of rules, blocks what looks destructive or would move data out of the repository, and lets everything else run without asking. That trades your attention for a filter that does not know your data or your intent. It still asks when a rule says so or when you have told the agent not to do something, and Shift+Tab switches back to manual mode at any time. The habit is the same in both modes: read what the agent proposes before it happens, or what it did right after.
The diff. Every change is visible before you accept it. An agent that edits ten files leaves ten diffs to read, and reading them is the practice this workshop asks of you.
The pull request. Changes reach main through a  and a reviewed . This is a working practice rather than an enforced setting, so it holds only as long as you follow it.

Git itself gives you the recovery path when something does slip through: committed work can be restored, which is the reason to  often while working with an agent.






ImportantThe short version



Bring openly shareable data. Assume anything in the project folder may be read. The plan you are on decides what happens to your sessions, and the group is settling that before the workshop.

title: Glossary
text:
The terms you meet during the pre-work and the workshop.
Each entry has two layers. The main text defines the term in plain, everyday words, so you can read it once and understand it. The quieter block underneath gives the more technical wording, which is the vocabulary you will meet in documentation and in other courses.
The page has four parts. Git and GitHub carries over the terms from the first workshop. Tools on your computer names the programs the pre-work installs. Working with agents covers the vocabulary this workshop adds. Research integrity has the words of the disclosure debate.
If you are unsure which tool a term belongs to, see Which tool does what?.
The Git and GitHub definitions draw on Glosario by The Carpentries, and the agent terms on the Dictionary of AI Coding. Full details are in References and attribution at the foot of the page.

title: Glossary
text:
Git and GitHub

branch

A branch is a separate line of work inside a repository. You create a branch when you want to change files without touching the main copy of the project. When the changes have been reviewed, you bring them back into the main copy. In the workshop you make your edits on a branch and bring them into main through a pull request.

Glosario: A snapshot of a version of a Git repository. Multiple branches can capture multiple versions of the same repository.


bug report

A description of an unexpected error or wrong output from a program, written down so that someone can find and fix the problem. On GitHub, bug reports are usually filed as issues.

clone

To clone a repository means to download a full copy of it from GitHub onto your own computer, including the record of every change ever made to it. You clone by running git clone in a terminal, or through your editor’s own Git menu.

Glosario: A copy (usually downloaded) of a Git remote repository on a local computer.


cloud

Computers, storage, and services that you reach over the internet instead of running on your own machine. When we say GitHub stores your repository in the cloud, we mean it stores the repository on GitHub’s servers.

commit

A commit is a saved version of your project. When you commit, Git records the exact content of your files at that moment, together with a message that says what you changed and why. You can go back to any earlier commit at any time.

Glosario: As a verb, the act of saving a set of changes to a version control repository. As a noun, the changes saved.


commit message

A commit message is the short note you attach to a commit. It tells your collaborators, and your future self, what you changed and why you changed it.

Glosario: A comment attached to a commit that explains what was done and why.


credential

A piece of information that proves to a computer system who you are, such as a password or a personal access token. Git keeps your GitHub credential on your computer, so you do not have to retype it for every push and pull.

default branch (main)

The default branch is the main copy of the project inside a repository, and it is usually called main. It should always hold a version of the project that works. You make changes on other branches and bring them into main after someone has reviewed them. In older projects the default branch is called master.

Glosario: A dedicated, permanent, central branch which should contain a ready product. After a new feature is developed on a separate branch, it can be merged into this branch.


dev branch

The branch we work on between releases. In this workshop your changes land on dev, get reviewed in a pull request, and reach main through the merge. You create dev once, in step 5, and it stays.

A long-lived integration branch. The name is a convention of this group, not a Git feature: Git treats dev like any other branch. See branching workflows in the Git book.


diff

A diff shows exactly what changed between two versions of a file, line by line: removed lines carry a minus, added lines a plus. Reading the diff is how you check what the agent did before you accept it.

Git produces diffs with git diff; the Git pane in RStudio and the Files changed tab of a pull request show the same output with colour. See git diff.


fork

A fork is a personal copy of someone else’s repository, stored in your own GitHub account. You can change your fork freely, and you can offer your changes back to the original repository through a pull request. We do not use forks in the workshop, because our teams share one repository and work on branches inside it.

Glosario: A copy of one person’s Git repository that lives in another person’s GitHub account. Changes to the content of a fork can be submitted to the upstream repository via a pull request.


Git

Git is a program on your computer that keeps track of changes to your files. It saves the versions you tell it to save, shows you what changed between versions, and lets you go back to any earlier version. Git works without an internet connection.

Glosario: A version control tool to record and manage changes to a project.


Git pane

Most editors, including RStudio and Positron, have a Git pane: a panel showing what has changed in your repository, with buttons for the everyday Git work. Every button runs a real Git command, so clicking Push runs git push. This workshop mostly uses the terminal instead, because that is where the agent works, but the two are interchangeable.

GitHub

GitHub is a website that stores a copy of your Git repository online, so that other people can see your project, download it, and work on it with you. GitHub also adds tools that Git itself does not have, such as pull requests and issues.

Glosario: A cloud-based platform built around Git that allows you to save versions of your project online and collaborate with other Git users.


history

The history is the ordered record of all commits made in a repository, from the very first commit to the newest. It shows who changed what, when, and why. Every clone contains the full history, which is why you can recover any earlier state of the project.

HTML

The format used for web pages. Rendering a Quarto document usually produces an HTML page that you can open in any web browser.

Glosario: The standard markup language used for web pages.


HTTPS

The secure way computers exchange data on the web, the same one behind every https:// address. Git talks to GitHub over HTTPS, which is why GitHub asks for a personal access token to prove who you are.

issue

An issue is a to-do item for a project, posted on the repository’s page on GitHub. An issue can describe a problem, ask for something new, or hold a task. You can assign an issue to a person, and you can refer to it from commits and pull requests.

Glosario: A bug report, feature request, or other to-do item associated with a project.


local repository

The local repository is the copy of a repository on your own computer, including the record of every change. Your commits are saved here first. Pushing then uploads them to the copy on GitHub.

Markdown

Markdown is a simple way to add formatting, such as headings, links, and lists, to ordinary text. You type plain characters, e.g. # in front of a heading, and the text is later shown with the formatting applied. GitHub uses Markdown in README files, issues, and pull requests, and Quarto uses it for the text in .qmd documents.

Glosario: A markup language with a simple syntax. Markdown is often used for README files.


markup language

A set of rules for marking up text to say what it means or how it should be shown. The marks themselves are usually not displayed. Markdown and HTML are markup languages.

Glosario: A set of rules for annotating text to define its meaning or how it should be displayed.


merge

To merge means to combine the changes from one branch into another, so that one branch now contains the work of both. In the workshop, the merge happens when a reviewer accepts a pull request on GitHub.

Glosario: Merging branches in Git incorporates the development histories of two branches in one. If changes are made to similar parts of both branches, a conflict will occur.


merge conflict

A merge conflict happens when two branches have changed the same lines of the same file, and Git cannot tell which version you want to keep. Git stops, marks both versions inside the file, and waits for you to choose or combine them. A conflict is not an error. It only means that Git will not guess which change you meant.

Glosario: A situation in which incompatible or overlapping changes have been made on different branches that are now being merged.


metadata

Information that describes other information. The author, date, and message attached to each commit are metadata about the changes in that commit.

open source

Software whose source code is public and licensed so that anyone may use, change, and share it. Git and Quarto are open source. GitHub is not, although it hosts millions of open-source projects.

origin

Origin is the name your computer uses for the copy of your repository on GitHub. Git sets the name automatically when you clone, so that you can push and pull without typing the full web address every time.

Glosario: A short name for a remote repository.


personal access token (PAT)

A personal access token is a long password that GitHub generates for you. Git sends it to GitHub when you push or pull, to prove that the request really comes from you. You created one during the Git for Scientists pre-work, and it should still work for this workshop.

plain text

Text stored as ordinary characters only, with no hidden formatting, so that any editor on any computer can open it. Git works best with plain text, because it can show exactly which lines changed between versions. Quarto documents, R scripts, and CSV files are all plain text.

pull

To pull means to download the newest commits from GitHub into the copy on your own computer, so that both copies are the same again. Pulling is the first step of the commit cycle. Pull, then stage, then commit, then push.

Glosario: Downloads and synchronizes changes between a remote repository and a local repository.


pull request

A pull request is a page on GitHub where you ask another person to review the changes on your branch and, if the changes are good, to merge the branch into main. The reviewer can read every changed line, write comments, and suggest edits. A pull request is not the same as a pull. A pull downloads commits to your computer, and a pull request is a conversation about merging.

Glosario: The request to merge a new feature or correction created on a branch or fork of a Git repository into the upstream repository. The developer is notified of the change, reviews it, makes or suggests changes, and potentially merges it.


push

To push means to upload your commits from your own computer to the copy of your repository on GitHub. Until you push, your commits exist only on your computer, and nobody else can see them.

Glosario: Uploads and synchronizes changes between a local repository and a remote repository.


Quarto

Quarto is a program that turns a text file into a finished document, such as a report, a website, or slides. A Quarto file ends in .qmd and contains ordinary text, code, and a few settings at the top. When you click Render, Quarto runs the code and builds the document. Quarto does not track versions and does not talk to GitHub.

README

A README is a text file that explains what a project is and how to use it. GitHub shows the file named README.md on the front page of the repository.

Glosario: A plain text file containing important information about a project or software package.


remote repository

The remote repository is the copy of a repository that is not on your computer. For us, the remote repository is the copy on GitHub. Pull and push move commits between your local copy and the remote copy, so that everyone can share their work.

Glosario: A repository located on another computer. Tools such as Git are designed to synchronize changes between local and remote repositories in order to share work.


render

To render means to have Quarto build the output document, e.g. a web page or a PDF, from a .qmd file. Rendering also runs the code inside the file. You render by running quarto render in a terminal, or by clicking Render in your editor.

repository

A repository is the folder for one project, together with the full record of every change made to the files in it. Git keeps the record in a hidden part of the folder. As a rule, one project gets one repository.

Glosario: A place where a version control system stores the files that make up a project and the metadata that describes their history.


server

A computer, or a program running on it, that provides data or services to other computers over a network. The remote copies of your repositories live on GitHub’s servers.

Glosario: Typically, a program such as a database manager or web server that provides data to a client upon request.


snapshot

The complete state of all files in your project at one moment in time, saved so that you can return to it later. Every commit stores a snapshot, and the history is the ordered line of those snapshots.

stage / staging area

To stage a file means to mark it for the next commit, and the staging area is where Git keeps the marked files until you commit. Git only commits the files you have staged, so you can change five files and commit only two of them. You stage a file with git add, or by ticking its checkbox in an editor’s Git pane.

synchronize

To bring two copies of the same thing to the same state, so that neither is missing changes the other has. Pull and push are how you synchronize your local repository with the remote repository on GitHub.

version control

Version control is a way of working where a program records every saved version of your files, so that you can see what changed, when, and why, and go back to any earlier version. Git is the version control program we use.

Glosario: A system for managing changes made to software during its development.


YAML

YAML is a simple format for settings, written as names and values. The block between the two --- lines at the top of a Quarto file is written in YAML, and it holds settings such as the title and the output format.

Glosario: Short for “YAML Ain’t Markup Language”, a way to represent nested data using indentation. YAML is often used in configuration files and to define parameters for various flavours of Markdown documents.

text:
Tools on your computer
The programs the pre-work installs or relies on, and the words the instructions use for parts of them.

Better BibTeX

A Zotero plugin that gives every item in your library a short, stable citation key, such as forte2022building. Step 7 installs it and sets the key formula the group shares.

Better BibTeX for Zotero generates and pins citation keys and exports BibTeX and BibLaTeX for LaTeX, Quarto and Markdown workflows.


citation key

A short ID for one reference, built from the first author, the year and the first word of the title, like forte2022building. Plain text documents cite by key, so a key must never change once other files use it.

In Quarto and Pandoc a citation is written [@forte2022building] and resolved against a bibliography file at render time. See citations in the Quarto guide.


Console

The pane in RStudio where you type R commands and see their output, at the bottom left by default, with a > prompt. It is not the Terminal tab next to it, which runs shell commands rather than R.

One of the four RStudio panes; see the RStudio user guide.


GitHub CLI

A program called gh that talks to GitHub from the terminal: it logs you in, opens issues and pull requests, and lists repositories. On the day the agent uses it to open issues and pull requests for you.

GitHub CLI. gh auth login stores a token for Git and the CLI; gh issue create and gh pr create are the two commands the workshop relies on.


Homebrew

The package manager for the Mac. One command in the terminal installs a program, one command updates it. It is installed once, from brew.sh, and step 5 uses it for the GitHub CLI.

Homebrew installs into /opt/homebrew on Apple silicon; brew install, brew upgrade.


mcptools

An R package that lets the agent reach into your running RStudio session: it can look at the objects there and run R code in it. Step 6 installs it and registers it with Claude Code.

mcptools implements the Model Context Protocol in R. mcp_server() runs the server that Claude Code talks to; mcp_session() registers a live R session with it.


PowerShell

The terminal program built into Windows, where you type commands. Its prompt starts with PS. The pre-work uses it for the install lines on Windows.

PowerShell is a shell and a scripting language. Windows also has the older Command Prompt, cmd, whose commands differ; the install lines on the pre-work pages are written for PowerShell.


Quick Copy

A Zotero setting that decides what lands on your clipboard when you copy an item. Step 7 sets it to the citation key, so Cmd+Shift+C on the Mac or Ctrl+Shift+C on Windows copies the key.

Quick Copy in the Zotero documentation.


R profile

A file called .Rprofile in your home folder that R reads every time it starts. Step 6 adds one line to it, so every RStudio session announces itself to the agent.

One of R’s startup files; see R startup in the R manual.


R session

One running copy of R together with everything you have loaded into it: packages, data frames, variables. RStudio starts one for you, and Session, Restart R gives you a fresh one.

The agent has no R session of its own. It can run scripts and render documents, but it sees the objects in a session only through the connection that mcptools provides.


RStudio

The program most of this group writes R in. Its window has four panes: the editor, the Console, the Environment and history, and Files, plots, packages and Git.

RStudio by Posit. Positron and VS Code are alternatives that the pre-work instructions do not cover.


shell

The program inside a terminal that reads what you type and runs it. On the Mac that is zsh, on Windows PowerShell or, with Git for Windows, Bash. Claude Code runs its own commands through a shell too.

Terminal and shell are often used for each other: the terminal is the window, the shell the program running in it. See the shell lesson by Software Carpentry.


terminal

A window where you type commands instead of clicking. Claude Code runs in one. Give it a window of its own next to your editor: the Terminal app on the Mac, PowerShell on Windows. RStudio’s Terminal tab also works, but it is slow and cramped for an agent.

See shell. The Claude Code documentation has a terminal guide for people who have never opened one.


uv

A small program that installs Python tools, including zotero-mcp, and takes care of Python for you. Step 8 installs it once.

uv by Astral. uv tool install installs a tool in its own environment and puts its command on your path.


Zotero Connector

The browser extension that saves the paper you are looking at into your Zotero library with one click. Step 7 installs it.

Zotero Connectors exist for Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Safari and hand items to the running Zotero app.


zotero-mcp

The small program that connects the agent to your Zotero library, so it can search the library and read the PDFs in it. Step 8 installs it and registers it with Claude Code.

zotero-mcp is an MCP server that talks to Zotero’s local API on your own computer; nothing leaves the machine except what the agent then sends to the model.

title: Glossary
text:
Working with agents

agent

An agent is a language model that has been given tools and set to work in a loop: it does something, looks at the result, decides what to do next, and repeats until the task is done or it needs you. Claude Code is an agent. A single question and answer is not an agent, because nothing happens in between.

A model, in a harness, that calls tools repeatedly in a loop, deciding each next step from the last result. Most agents carry read tools that observe and write tools that change things, giving the cycle explore, change, observe.


auto mode

The permission mode Claude Code starts in on the Team, Pro and Max plans. A second model, the classifier, checks each action and lets ordinary ones run without asking you. It blocks actions that look destructive or would send data out of the repository. We work in auto mode on the day.

Permission modes in the Claude Code documentation. Shift+Tab cycles between auto, manual, accept edits and plan mode.


classifier

The second model that reviews the agent’s actions in auto mode, against a set of rules, instead of you. It sees your messages and the agent’s tool calls, not the contents of files, so text inside a file cannot talk it into anything.

How the classifier evaluates actions in the Claude Code documentation. Blocked actions are listed under Recently denied in /permissions.


context window

The context window is everything the model can see while it answers: your instructions, the conversation so far, and the contents of any file that was read. It has a size limit. When a session runs long, early parts fall out of view, which is one reason a fresh session sometimes works better than a long one.

The full set of tokens sent to the model on a single request. Everything the model knows about your situation at that moment is inside it, and nothing outside it exists as far as the model is concerned.


hallucination

A hallucination is output that is stated confidently and is wrong. A model can invent a function that does not exist, a citation for a paper nobody wrote, or a plausible number. It does not signal uncertainty when it does this, which is why the output has to be checked by someone who could tell.

Confidently-wrong model output. Two variants are usually distinguished: factuality (the claim is false about the world) and faithfulness (the claim is not supported by the source it cites).


harness

The harness is the program wrapped around the model that turns it into an agent. It sends the requests, runs the tools on your computer, sends the results back, and asks you for permission. Claude Code is a harness. So is a chat window, though a much simpler one.

Everything around the model that turns it into an agent: the loop, the tool definitions, the system prompt, the permission layer, and the context assembly.


inference

Inference is the model producing output. Training is what set the model’s numbers, months ago; inference is what happens each time you send a request. Nothing you do during inference changes the model.

Running a trained model to generate output, as distinct from training, which sets its parameters.


manual mode

The permission mode in which Claude Code asks you before every command and every file edit. From auto mode, one press of Shift+Tab gets you there, and the status line says so.

The configuration value is default; the documentation calls it Manual. See permission modes.


MCP (Model Context Protocol)

MCP is a standard way of giving an agent access to something outside your project folder, such as a reference manager, a database, or an issue tracker. A piece of software that offers such access is called an MCP server. We use one on the day to search literature through Zotero.

A protocol for exposing external tools to an agent through a server. Note the cost: an MCP server’s tool definitions are sent on every request, so a command-line tool the agent already knows how to run is often the cheaper choice.


model

The model is the part that does the reasoning. It runs on the provider’s servers, not on your machine, and it has no memory between requests. Everything it knows about your work was sent to it in that request.

A stateless set of parameters that performs next-token prediction. Statelessness is why the whole conversation is resent each time, and why costs grow over a long session.


permission

A permission prompt is the agent stopping to ask before it does something that changes the world: writing a file, running a command, making a commit. It is your decision point, and reading what is being proposed before approving is the habit that separates using an agent from hoping.

The harness gates tool calls that have side effects. Which calls are gated depends on the permission mode; approving one does not approve the next.


plan mode

A mode in which the agent reads and proposes but changes nothing. Use it to have the agent look at something, or to get a plan before any work starts. Press Shift+Tab until the status line says plan mode.

Plan mode in the Claude Code documentation. In plan mode the agent may run read-only commands; edits and other commands wait for you to leave it.


prompt

A prompt is what you type to the agent. It is a description of what you want, not a command with a fixed syntax, so being specific about what “done” looks like matters more than any particular wording.

The user-supplied portion of the request. It sits alongside the system prompt, the conversation history, and any tool results already in the context window.


sandbox

A sandbox is a restricted space the agent runs inside, so that a mistake cannot reach the rest of your computer. Git serves a similar purpose in a different way: it does not stop the agent from changing a file, but it lets you see exactly what changed and undo it.

An isolated environment limiting what an agent can read, write, or reach. Sandboxing, version control, and backups are the three standard mitigations for the fact that write tools are both the point and the risk.


session

A session is one continuous run of working with the agent, from starting it to closing it. Everything said in a session is in view; nothing carries into the next one unless it was written to a file.

One bounded run of interaction with an agent. Ending a session and starting fresh is the normal remedy when the context window has filled with material that is no longer relevant.


skill

A file of instructions the agent loads when a task matches the skill’s description, so you do not explain the same procedure every time. On the day we install two, one that commits and one that opens a pull request.

Skills in the Claude Code documentation. A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file; its description is always visible to the model, the body loads on demand.


system prompt

The system prompt is the standing instruction the harness sends with every request, telling the model what it is and how to behave. You do not usually see it. A CLAUDE.md file in your project is a way for you to add to it.

Instructions the harness prepends to every model request. Project-level files such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md are the user-editable layer on top of it.


token

A token is the unit a model reads and writes: roughly a short word or part of one. Everything is counted in tokens, including cost. This is the practical reason a long session gets more expensive than a short one, since the whole conversation is sent again each time.

The atomic unit of model input and output. Input tokens are what the harness sends, output tokens what the model generates; cached tokens are input the provider has stored from an earlier request and charges less for.


tool

A tool is a function the agent can call: read a file, write a file, run a command, search the web. The agent cannot do anything that is not one of its tools. The description of each tool is all the model knows about it.

A function the harness exposes to the model, described by a name, a description, and an input schema. Read tools observe; write tools change things.


tool call

A tool call is the agent asking for a tool to be run, with particular arguments. The harness runs it and sends back the result. Most of what you see scrolling past during an agent session is tool calls and their results.

The model’s output naming a tool and its arguments, rather than text for the user. The harness executes it and returns a tool result into the context window.


trailer

A line at the end of a commit message in the form Key: value, such as Assisted-by: Claude. Trailers mark which commits an agent touched, and Git can list and count them.

git interpret-trailers. git log --grep='^Assisted-by:' finds every commit that carries the trailer.


vibe coding

Vibe coding means prompting for code and accepting what comes back without properly reading it. Andrej Karpathy named it for throwaway work where that is fine. The name is also used loosely for any AI-assisted coding, which muddies a distinction worth keeping: whether anyone actually checked.

Coined by Karpathy for low-stakes work where the code is not reviewed. The contrasting practice, sometimes called agentic engineering, keeps the review step and treats the agent as a collaborator whose output goes through the same scrutiny as a colleague’s.

title: Glossary
text:
Research integrity
The words of the disclosure debate, as the background pages use them.

content credentials

Signed information attached to an image or other file that records how it was made, including whether an AI tool produced it. Claude attaches them to the images it makes. They live in the file’s metadata and are lost when the file is re-saved without them.

The C2PA standard, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity.


data package

A dataset published together with its documentation: what each column means, where the data came from, how it was cleaned, in a form both people and programs can read. The workshop compares what an agent does with a plain CSV against the same data as a package.

In this group a data package is an R package built with the openwashdata tooling. The wider idea is the Frictionless Data Package, a folder of data files with a machine-readable description.


declaration

The statement in a paper, thesis or talk that says which AI tools you used, for what, and what you did yourself. ETH asks for one, and the record your workflow leaves behind is what you write it from.

The ETH Library’s citation guide sets out the form of the declaration; see the references page.


disclosure

Telling the reader that AI was used, and how. The word the journals and research integrity bodies use for the rules they are writing; a declaration is the text you write to meet them.

The Round 2 consultation document of the global reporting standard defines disclosure as information about the use of AI provided in the research article for transparency; see the references page.


watermark

A hidden pattern in text produced by a language model that a detector can recognise, so the text can be traced to a machine. Claude’s text carries one since August 2026. It says that a machine was involved, and nothing about who decided what.

Anthropic’s page on how Claude’s text watermark works. Images carry content credentials instead.

title: Which tool does what?
text:
During the workshop several tools appear on your screen at the same time, and their names sound alike. It is completely normal to lose track of which one is doing what.
The first half covers Git, GitHub, and Quarto, carried over from the Git for Scientists workshop. The second half adds the .

title: Which tool does what?
section: The tools in one sentence each
text:
The tools in one sentence each
Git is a  program that runs on your computer. It records the  of your files: every commit, every , every . Git works even without an internet connection.
GitHub is a website (github.com) that hosts a copy of your Git  in the cloud. Everything that involves other people happens here: pull requests, reviews, issues, and forks. GitHub is built on top of Git, but it is a separate product made by a separate company.
Quarto is a publishing program that turns a plain-text document (a .qmd file) into a finished report, website, or presentation. When you , Quarto runs your code and builds the output document. Quarto knows nothing about version control.
Claude Code is the agent. It reads and writes files in your project folder, runs commands, and uses Git on your behalf. It runs on your computer, in a .
The model (Claude) is the part that does the reasoning. It runs on Anthropic’s servers, not on your machine. It has no memory between sessions and no access to your files; everything it knows about your work, Claude Code had to send it.

title: Which tool does what?
text:
A rule of thumb

If it records or moves the history of your files, it is Git.
If it involves another person or a web browser, it is GitHub.
If it turns text and code into a document, it is Quarto.
If it decides what to do next, it is the model.
If it actually does it on your machine, it is Claude Code.

title: Which tool does what?
section: The three kinds of AI coding tool
text:
The three kinds of AI coding tool
People say “AI coding tool” for three quite different things, and the difference matters when you choose one.








Kind
What it does
Examples




Autocomplete
Suggests the next few lines as you type. You stay in control of every keystroke.
GitHub Copilot


AI editor
An editor with a chat panel that can edit files for you, inside that editor.
Cursor, Positron Assistant


Agentic coding
Runs on its own for many steps: reads files, runs commands, uses Git, decides what to do next from what it finds.
Claude Code, Codex CLI



This workshop is about the third kind. The difference is not that the agent is cleverer; it is that it acts in a loop without asking you at every step, which is what makes it useful and what makes the record of what it did necessary.

title: Which tool does what?
text:
Where MCP fits
You will hear MCP (Model Context Protocol) mentioned. It is a way of giving the agent access to something outside your project folder, such as a reference manager or a running . The pre-work sets up two such connections: one to your R session in step 6, one to your Zotero library in step 8.

title: Which tool does what?
text:
Common mix-ups
Claude Code is not the model. Claude Code is the program on your computer that reads files, runs commands, and asks . The model is the thing on Anthropic’s servers that decides what to do. When the agent does something odd, it is usually worth asking which of the two is responsible: a wrong decision is the model, a refused action is Claude Code doing its job.
The agent is not remembering you. Each request sends the whole conversation again, because the model keeps nothing between requests. This is why a long session costs more than a short one, and why starting fresh sometimes fixes a session that has gone in circles.
Asking is not doing. The agent proposes; you approve. Every permission prompt is a decision point, and clicking through them without reading is how people end up with changes they did not want. In , which we use on the day, a built-in check takes most of those decisions, and the  becomes the point where you decide.
Commit is not push. Unchanged from July. The agent committing means the change is saved on your computer. Until something pushes, nobody else can see it.
An agent using Git does not make the work traceable on its own. The history is only useful if the commits are honest about what changed and who asked for it. Letting an agent write commits is highly effective, because it describes the changes well. Those are part of the transparency and provenance questions the workshop works on.
If a term on this page is unfamiliar, look it up in the glossary.

Claude Code is the coding  we use on the day. It runs in a , works inside the folder you start it in, reads and edits files there, and runs commands. It asks before it runs a command or changes a file, and that  prompt is the first thing to learn to read.

title: Step 4: Install Claude Code and log in
text:
Part 1: Your Claude account
Claude Code is not part of the free Claude plan. You need one of the two routes below.

GHE membersEveryone else


You will receive an email invitation to the Global Health Engineering organization on the Claude Team plan, sent to your ETH email address. Accept it. If you do not have a Claude account under that address yet, the invitation walks you through creating one.
Use your ETH address, not a personal one. If you already use Claude with a personal address, the Team seat is a separate account and you log into Claude Code with the ETH one.
The invitation expires after three weeks. If none has arrived by the time you reach this step, tell me in the chat room.
On the Team plan, what you type and what the agent reads is not used to train models, and the group, not the vendor, controls the data. That is the reason for the plan.


Create your own account at claude.ai and subscribe to a paid plan for the month of the workshop. The Pro plan is enough. I suggest the Max plan for one month, since the day involves a lot of agent work and the Pro limits can run out in an afternoon. Cancel afterwards if you do not want to keep it.
Then do one thing before anything else: open your privacy settings and turn off the setting that allows your chats and coding sessions to be used for model training. On the Free, Pro and Max plans that setting is on unless you turn it off, and it covers Claude Code sessions. With the setting off, your data is kept for 30 days instead of five years and is not used for training.

claude --version

The first prints a version number. The second checks the installation and prints what it found. Both should finish without an error.

For working with Claude Code, give it a terminal window of its own next to your editor, not the Terminal tab inside RStudio, which is slow and cramped; Part 3 shows the layout. On the Mac, iTerm is a good alternative to the built-in Terminal; if you are interested in using it, get in touch. section: Part 3: Clone your setup repository and log in
text:
Part 3: Clone your setup repository and log in

Clone your setup repository
I have created a repository for you in the organization, named setup-USERNAME with your GitHub username in place of USERNAME. It holds a small public dataset and one R script, and it is where every test before the day runs.

Open the organization page, https://github.com/agentsforsci-ghe/, and find setup-USERNAME in the list of repositories. Use the search field on that page if the list is long.
Open it, click the green Code button, and copy the HTTPS URL.
In RStudio, choose File, New Project, Version Control, Git, paste the URL, and under Create project as subdirectory of browse to Documents/gitrepos/gh-org-agentsforsci-ghe, creating that folder if it does not exist yet. Then click Create Project. This is the same  you did in the first workshop; the instructions from then still apply, screenshots included.

RStudio opens the new project. The Files pane at the bottom right shows 01-read-data.R, a data folder, and a .






NoteWhere repositories live



The folder structure from the first workshop carries on. Every Git repository lives under Documents/gitrepos, in one folder per GitHub organization named gh-org- plus the organization, and one folder per personal account named gh- plus the username. So this workshop’s repositories go into gh-org-agentsforsci-ghe, next to the gh-org-gitforsci-ghe folder from July, and a personal website cloned from your own account would go into gh-rainbow-train, with your username in place of rainbow-train. Keep gitrepos out of folders that sync to a  drive.








ImportantNo repository with your name



Tell me in the chat room. Creating it takes me a minute.




Open a terminal at that folder
Claude Code works in the folder you start it from, so the terminal has to be opened inside the setup repository. Give it a terminal window of its own and put it next to RStudio: the two windows side by side, filling the screen, the editor on one side and the agent on the other. That is the layout for the whole day. RStudio and other editors have a terminal built in, and it does work, but it is slow and cramped for an agent, so keep it as a fallback.

macOS FinderWindows ExplorerRStudio, as a fallback


Open Finder and go to the folder you just created, Documents/gitrepos/gh-org-agentsforsci-ghe/setup-USERNAME. Right-click the folder and choose New Terminal at Folder. A Terminal window opens inside it. If the entry is missing from the menu, look under Services in the same menu, or switch it on once under System Settings, Keyboard, Keyboard Shortcuts, Services, Files and Folders.


Open File Explorer and open the folder you just created. Right-click an empty area inside the folder and choose Open in Terminal. On Windows 10, hold Shift while right-clicking and choose Open PowerShell window here. Open Git Bash here, which Git for Windows added to the same menu, works as well.


With the project open, choose Tools, Terminal, New Terminal. A Terminal tab appears next to the , already inside the project folder. It works on both systems, and it is the slow, cramped option: use it only when the other two fail.



Whichever way you chose, the prompt in the terminal ends with the folder name, setup-USERNAME. If it does not, you are in the wrong folder. Now place the terminal window and the RStudio window side by side and make them fill the screen.


Log in

In that terminal, start Claude Code:
claude
The first start asks you to pick a colour theme, then opens your browser to log in. Log in with the account from Part 1. If the browser does not open, press c to copy the login link and paste it into a browser yourself. GHE members: if asked which organization to use, pick Global Health Engineering.
Back in the terminal, type /status and press Enter. It shows which account you are logged in with. Check that it is the one you intended.
Look at the bottom line of the window, where Claude Code shows its permission mode. On the Team, Pro and Max plans it starts in auto mode: a built-in check approves ordinary actions on its own and asks you only when something looks risky. Pressing Shift+Tab switches to manual mode, where it asks before every command. Either is fine for the pre-work. On the workshop day we work in .
Say hello. Type a greeting and press Enter. You get a greeting back. That is the whole test.
Type /exit to leave.

Do not ask it to do anything else yet. Step 9 is where you give it work, with the safety rails in place.






NoteWhy a setup repository and not your own



The agent reads whole folders and sends what it finds to a model. Before the day, it does not see the data you committed in step 1. Every test in steps 4 to 9 runs in setup-USERNAME, which holds public data prepared for exactly this. We set the safety rails for your own repository together in the room.
